cim_eredeti: VR pioneer Jaron Lanier says Silicon Valley is sabotaging itself by poorly pitching AI and treating areas designated for data centers as sacrifice zones (Jaron Lanier/New York Times)
szoveg_eredeti:
Silicon Valley has a special talent for offering amazing products and then screwing them up with ridiculous ideas about how those products should be used.

Few appreciate virtual reality more than I do. I came up with the term. There are simple pleasures in occasionally visiting alternate sensory worlds. It was only when virtual reality went mainstream around 2013 that I realized Americans would not embrace the technology for a generation. The reason: the awful ways key tech leaders talked about it. Recall the Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg proclaiming that we would primarily live our lives through virtual reality headsets. Or the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen suggesting that most people were doomed to live virtually, with only elites retaining the privilege of living in the physical world. Predictably, the public did not embrace this vision.

We in Silicon Valley are doing it again with artificial intelligence, except worse — and at a larger scale. In its filing for its upcoming trillion-plus-dollar initial public offering, the leading A.I. lab Anthropic warned that its models could present “catastrophic or existential risks.”

I work on A.I. and use it and like it. The latest large models are genuinely useful. But rather than focusing on how these tools could improve lives, many leaders at the biggest A.I. companies are instead asking Americans to embrace the belief that this technology may kill us and our children, or at the very least drain us of all potential for livelihood and meaning. It should not be surprising then that based on the results of this last election, many Americans have come to disapprove of A.I. more than almost anything.

This disapproval is unfortunate and unnecessary. It does not arise from the technology itself. It is a reaction to the insular culture surrounding A.I., a culture that is dictating how this innovation is packaged, how it is sold and how it is understood. Words have a way of filtering into actions, as when some of us in Silicon Valley callously treat places where we want to build data centers as sacrifice zones. We technologists are sabotaging ourselves, but it is hard to find a sane focus from inside the intensity and elite isolation of this bubble. Americans are not rejecting A.I. They are rejecting the way Silicon Valley is defining it for them.

I have been discussing A.I. with some of its founding fathers for decades. In the 1980s, I think I coined the phrase “tools not creatures” in one of the arguments I had with my mentor Marvin Minsky, the MIT professor who was instrumental in shaping A.I. culture. Since there is no definitive evidence proving that A.I. is a conscious entity, the phrase means that I am entirely within my rights — as is anyone else within theirs — to think of the technology as more akin to a fancy calculator than, say, a German shepherd. That choice helps us design more useful products. And, as we’ll see, it provides a concrete and achievable way to make A.I. safe.
